posts.title: Advisory CL-2026-014: critical remote code execution in edge VPN appliances
posts.excerpt: A pre-authentication flaw in a widely deployed family of edge VPN appliances is being exploited. Patch or isolate today.
posts.content:
The vendor has disclosed a vulnerability in the web portal of its edge VPN appliances that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code on the device. Exploitation in the wild was confirmed on 23 October and public proof-of-concept code is circulating.

What to do now

  1. Upgrade to firmware 9.4.2 or later. The update takes about ten minutes and needs one reboot.
  2. If you cannot patch today, disable the web portal on the external interface.
  3. Reset the local administrator password and review VPN accounts created in the last 30 days.
  4. Check the appliance logs for requests to unusual portal paths since 15 October.

How we responded

Our security operations team patched all managed appliances within six hours of the vendor release and found no signs of compromise. We will keep monitoring for related activity and update this advisory if anything changes.

If you are not a Cloudline client and need help checking an appliance, call our incident line. We will tell you honestly whether you need us.

comments.content: Thanks for the clear steps. We are not clients but your workaround got us through the night.

posts.title: Advisory CL-2026-012: high-severity privilege escalation in shared print servers
posts.excerpt: A local privilege escalation in the print spooler lets any signed-in user become an administrator. The monthly update fixes it.
posts.content:
This month’s operating system update fixes a flaw in the print spooler that lets a signed-in user run code with system privileges. It is not remotely exploitable on its own, but attackers often chain this kind of bug with a phishing foothold.

Recommended actions

  • Apply the October cumulative update to every server with the print role.
  • Disable the spooler service on servers that do not print, including domain controllers.
  • Restrict driver installation to administrators with group policy.

We will update this advisory if exploitation is reported. Clients will see the patch status for each server in their monthly report.

Most small offices only need one print server. If yours has several, this is a good moment to consolidate.

posts.title: Case study: moving a regional logistics firm to the cloud in 90 days
posts.excerpt: Fourteen ageing servers, three depots and a dispatch system that could not go down. Here is how we moved it all without a missed delivery.
posts.content:
A family-owned logistics company with three depots ran its dispatch, accounts and file shares on fourteen servers in a back office. The hardware was out of warranty and the last full restore test was a memory.

14 → 3

servers after consolidation

31%

lower monthly running cost

0

missed deliveries during the move

The approach

  • Weeks 1–2: inventory, dependency mapping and a tested backup of everything.
  • Weeks 3–6: file shares and email first, because they are easiest to roll back.
  • Weeks 7–11: accounts and dispatch, moved over two Sunday nights.
  • Week 12: old servers wiped, recycled and certificates issued.

Monday after the dispatch move, the drivers didn’t notice anything. That was the whole point.

Operations director, client

The company now runs on Cloudline’s Professional plan, with monthly cost reviews that have found further savings each quarter.

posts.title: Case study: a 40-seat clinic gets ransomware-ready backups
posts.excerpt: Immutable copies, a four-hour restore target and a rehearsal every quarter turned backups from a hope into a plan.
posts.content:
A private clinic with forty staff relied on a single network drive that copied itself to a USB disk every night. When a neighbouring practice was hit by ransomware, the partners asked a simple question: how long would it take us to come back?

What we changed

  • Nightly backups to two locations, one of them immutable for 30 days.
  • Patient records replicated every fifteen minutes.
  • A documented four-hour restore target for the scheduling system.

Proving it works

Every quarter we restore the scheduling system to an isolated network and time it. The first rehearsal took five hours and forty minutes; the latest took two hours and ten.

The clinic also passed its regulator’s data protection review with no findings, using the reports our platform produces each month.

posts.title: Case study: retail chain cuts helpdesk tickets by 38%
posts.excerpt: Twenty-two shops, one overworked IT manager and a ticket queue that never emptied. Most of the fix was standardisation.
posts.content:
A chain of twenty-two homeware shops had grown by acquisition, and every shop had a slightly different till, router and laptop. The in-house IT manager spent his days on the phone instead of on projects.

Standardise, then automate

We replaced routers shop by shop overnight, rebuilt laptops from two standard images and set up self-service password resets, which alone removed a fifth of all tickets.

What the IT manager does now

He runs the projects he was hired for, starting with a new stock system, while our helpdesk handles the day-to-day.

posts.title: Zero trust for small businesses, without the buzzwords
posts.excerpt: Zero trust sounds like an enterprise programme. For a twenty-person company it comes down to five practical habits.
posts.content:
The idea behind zero trust is simple: being on the office network should not make a device or a person trusted. For a small business, that translates into a handful of changes you can make this quarter.

Five habits

  1. Phishing-resistant sign-in for email and admin accounts.
  2. Managed devices only for company data, checked at every sign-in.
  3. Least privilege: nobody uses an admin account for daily work.
  4. Segment the network so guest Wi-Fi and printers cannot reach laptops.
  5. Log and alert on sign-ins from new countries and devices.

None of these require new hardware. Most are settings in tools you already pay for, and together they block the attacks we see most often.

Security isn’t a product you buy, it’s a set of defaults you stop compromising on.

Head of security operations

posts.title: The 3-2-1-1 backup rule, explained
posts.excerpt: Three copies, two media, one off-site, one immutable. Why the extra one matters now, and how to check yours in an afternoon.
posts.content:
The classic 3-2-1 rule served businesses well for decades. Ransomware changed the threat: attackers now look for backups first and encrypt or delete them before anything else.

The rule

  • 3 copies of your data
  • 2 different kinds of storage
  • 1 copy off-site
  • 1 copy immutable or offline

Check yours this afternoon

Pick one important file from last Tuesday and try to restore it without help. Time it. If it takes more than an hour or you are not sure which copy is the newest, your backups need attention.

If you want a second pair of eyes, our engineers run a free backup review for organisations under fifty people.

posts.title: Our new network operations centre is live
posts.excerpt: A second operations centre in Easton gives every client geographic redundancy and our night shift a much better coffee machine.
posts.content:
This month we opened our second network operations centre, in Easton. It mirrors the Lakeport site, so either can run all of our monitoring and support on its own.

What it means for clients

  • No single building can take our support offline.
  • Night-shift handovers happen between sites, so engineers are fresh.
  • Monitoring data is stored in two regions.

Both sites run on independent power and network providers, and we test a full failover from one to the other every quarter.

We are hiring engineers for both sites. If you like solving problems before anyone notices them, say hello.
